statement: In women in the general population who were pregnant or had recently given birth, any alcohol use during pregnancy, as reported in studies published from 1984 to mid-2014 (328 studies with data from 50 countries; studies of special populations, such as Indigenous women, adolescents and women with an alcohol use disorder, left out, although the review notes that drinking in pregnancy can be much higher in some such groups), was estimated in one systematic review with meta-analysis and modelling (Popova et al., 2017; funded by the authors' institute, with no external funding sought; no competing interests declared) at 9.8% worldwide (95% CI 8.9% to 11.1%), about 10 in 100 pregnant women, in estimates labelled 2012 and weighted by live births. By WHO region it was 10.0% (8.5% to 11.8%) in the African region, 11.2% (9.4% to 12.6%) in the Americas, 0.2% (0.1% to 0.9%) in the Eastern Mediterranean, 25.2% (21.6% to 29.6%) in the European region, about 25 in 100, 1.8% (0.9% to 5.1%) in South-East Asia and 8.6% (4.5% to 11.6%) in the Western Pacific; country estimates ran from 0% (five countries, all by prediction) to 60.4% (42.8% to 76.8%), and the five highest were all in the European region. Most of these figures are model estimates, not measurements: studies were pooled for 29 countries, and the other 158, including 21 of the 50 countries with data (editors' arithmetic), were given a value predicted from national income, women's average alcohol consumption and WHO region. The data are self-reports, which the authors say may undercount drinking; the amount and frequency of drinking, and so binge drinking, were not analysed because the studies reported them inconsistently or not at all, timing in pregnancy was not analysed either, and no drink size is defined; and studies published over three decades are pooled into one set of figures labelled 2012 (editors' observation). Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: One large review estimated that about 10 in 100 pregnant women worldwide drank some alcohol during pregnancy, from under 1 in 100 in the WHO Eastern Mediterranean region to about 25 in 100 in the European region. Only 29 countries had enough studies to pool; the figures for the other 158 countries came from a model. Women reported their own drinking, so it may be undercounted, and the review did not look at how much or when women drank. Groups who may drink more, such as adolescents or women with an alcohol use disorder, were left out, and the studies span 30 years.
population: Women in the general population of each country who were pregnant or had recently given birth, in studies published from January 1984 to June 2014 (328 studies, 50 countries in all six WHO regions); studies of special populations (for example Indigenous women, adolescents, women of low socioeconomic status, women with HIV or with an alcohol use disorder) and studies that left out women who did not drink were excluded; estimates for 187 WHO member states
exposure: Any alcohol use at any time in pregnancy, as reported by the women (mostly questionnaires or interviews); amount, frequency, binge drinking and timing not analysed; no drink size defined
comparator: None (a prevalence: the share of pregnant women who drank)
outcome: Prevalence of any alcohol use during pregnancy (%), by country, WHO region and worldwide, weighted by live births and labelled 2012
magnitude: Popova et al. 2017, Table (any alcohol use during pregnancy in the general population, 2012, weighted by live births; 95% CI by Monte Carlo simulation): worldwide 9.8% (8.9–11.1); WHO African region 10.0% (8.5–11.8); Americas 11.2% (9.4–12.6); Eastern Mediterranean 0.2% (0.1–0.9); European 25.2% (21.6–29.6); South-East Asia 1.8% (0.9–5.1); Western Pacific 8.6% (4.5–11.6). The five highest countries, in alphabetical order: Belarus 46.6% (42.4–50.7; predicted), Denmark 45.8% (30.9–61.2), Ireland 60.4% (42.8–76.8), Russia 36.5% (18.7–56.4), UK 41.3% (lower limit 32.9; upper limit misprinted); 0% (predicted) in Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. Pooled by random-effects meta-analysis for 29 countries; predicted by fractional response regression for 158. As counts: about 10 in 100 pregnant women worldwide and about 25 in 100 in the European region (editors' rounding).

evidence.locator: Results, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Methods › Meta-analyses, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Of 23,470 records, 328 studies were retained, with general-population data from 50 countries in all six WHO regions. Prevalence was pooled by country-specific random-effects meta-analysis for 29 countries and predicted for 158 countries with one or no study (or a pooled interval of 0 to 100%) by fractional response regression on GDP per capita at purchasing power parity, women's mean total alcohol consumption and WHO region (Europe split into EU and non-EU states, the Americas into Canada and the USA against the rest); the predictions were made for the year 2012. Editors' arithmetic: 21 of the 50 countries with data (50 minus 29) were given predicted values in place of their observed ones.

evidence.locator: Methods › Search strategy and selection criteria, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 3rd paragraph
evidence.extracted: Studies of alcohol use in pregnancy published from 1 January 1984 to 30 June 2014 were searched in 14 databases without language or geographic restriction. Excluded: studies that left out women who did not drink, samples from special populations (for example Indigenous women, adolescents, women of low socioeconomic status, women with HIV and women with an alcohol use disorder), pooled estimates and duplicate publications. Where a study gave several estimates, preference went to the one after pregnancy was recognised, over the whole pregnancy, within 6 weeks after the birth, or by a validated method. The Discussion notes that drinking in pregnancy has been reported to be much higher in some at-risk populations, citing 60.5% among Inuit women in northern Quebec, over ten times the estimate for Canada's general population.

evidence.extracted: Limitations stated by the authors: some included studies used non-representative samples or unvalidated tools; drinking was self-reported and open to reporting and recall bias, so drinking (and FAS) may be underestimated; drinking patterns (frequency and quantity) were not analysed because they were not reported or were reported inconsistently; predicted values may differ from the true prevalence because of measurement error and omitted variables such as alcohol policies; only WHO member states were covered.

risk_of_bias.note: Drinking was self-reported, which the authors say is open to reporting and recall bias, so the figures are more likely too low than too high; some included studies used non-representative samples or unvalidated questions. AMSTAR 2 critically low on the card (sc_popova_2017): protocol registered after the searches had closed, no list of excluded studies, heterogeneity and publication-bias results only in the appendix, observed single-study values replaced by predictions.

inconsistency.note: Not downgraded: country estimates run from 0% to 60.4%, which reflects differences between countries and is reported by region rather than as one number; heterogeneity within countries is reported only in the appendix (not read).

indirectness.note: Most country figures, and so most of each regional and the world figure, are model predictions rather than measurements (158 of 187 countries, including 21 with a single study); one set of figures labelled 2012 pools studies published from 1984 to 2014.

imprecision.note: Not downgraded: the world interval is narrow (8.9% to 11.1%); the wider regional intervals (Western Pacific 4.5% to 11.6%, South-East Asia 0.9% to 5.1%) are reported; the Monte Carlo intervals leave out the error of the prediction model, which is counted under indirectness.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable: funnel-plot and regression tests were run, with results only in the appendix (not read).

grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim (a prevalence), rated as a description of the population sampled: it starts low (METHODS §6.3) and is never upgraded. Rated down once for risk of bias (self-reported drinking could move the figures materially, most likely upwards) and once for indirectness (most country, regional and world figures are model predictions, not measurements), so very low. Status single study: the figures are one review's pooled and modelled estimates; its 328 primary studies are independent of one another, but their results appear only in the appendix (not read), and no other global estimate was read. The companion FASD review (Lange et al., 2017) builds on these drinking estimates and is not independent evidence for them. The paper's 2017 correction concerns only its two maps, from which no figure here is taken.
